excerpt: Day porter pricing is quoted three ways—hourly, per square foot per month, and per fixture—and each hides different assumptions. This guide gives US office managers national unit prices, minimum charges, and worked monthly budgets for part-time and full-time coverage.
quickAnswer: Day porter services in the US typically bill at $35–$65 per porter hour, which works out to about $1,520–$2,820 per month for a 2-hour weekday shift, $3,030–$5,630 for a 4-hour part-time shift, and $6,060–$11,260 for a full-time 8-hour porter at 4.33 weeks per month. On a per-square-foot basis that usually lands between $0.10 and $0.30 per sq ft per month depending on building size, with per-visit minimums of $90–$135 for short call-in shifts.

blocks.text: What You Are Actually Buying With a Day Porter

A day porter is a janitorial worker stationed in your building during occupied hours. Nightly crews handle the deep, production-rate work—vacuuming every square foot, emptying every bin, scrubbing every restroom. The porter handles what breaks between those visits: restroom checks and restocking, lobby and entry floor touchups, breakroom resets after lunch, spill response, conference room turnovers, trash runs from high-volume areas, and visible-surface wipe-downs. Because porters are paid for presence rather than square footage covered, pricing behaves differently from standard office cleaning.

That distinction drives every pricing conversation. A nightly crew might cover 3,500 sq ft per hour under ISSA production standards, so a 20,000 sq ft office takes under six labor hours. A porter on the same site might work four hours and touch only the lobby, two restroom cores, and the kitchen. You are paying for responsiveness and appearance, not area. That is why the hourly rate is the anchor unit and per-sq-ft figures are derived from it.

blocks.text: The spread inside each range is mostly labor market and burden. A $35 per hour bill rate usually reflects a lower-wage metro, a non-union site, and a contractor that bundles the porter into an existing nightly contract. A $65 rate reflects higher local wages, full payroll burden (FICA, workers' compensation, unemployment insurance, paid leave), supervisor oversight, and equipment provided by the vendor. Credentialed porters in hospitals, outpatient clinics, labs, and federal-adjacent buildings land in the $55–$95 specialty bracket.

blocks.title: Benchmark: converting porter hours to per-sq-ft
blocks.text: A 4-hour weekday porter in a 20,000 sq ft office costs $3,031–$5,629 per month, or roughly $0.15–$0.28 per sq ft per month. A full-time porter in a 60,000 sq ft building costs $6,062–$11,258, or about $0.10–$0.19 per sq ft. Larger buildings dilute the fixed labor across more area, which is why per-sq-ft porter quotes fall as buildings grow.
Minimum Charges, Call-In Shifts, and Premiums

Short visits trigger minimums. Most contractors will not dispatch a porter for under two hours, and per-visit minimums of $90–$135 are common for event coverage, a single board-meeting day, or a one-off spill response. Same-day emergency calls often carry a 1.25x to 1.5x premium, and weekend or holiday shifts typically bill at time-and-a-half wage equivalents. If your contract includes a standing porter, negotiate that occasional extended hours bill at the base rate rather than the call-in rate.

items: Two-hour minimum per dispatch is standard; four-hour minimums are common in union buildings.
Weekend and holiday shifts usually bill 1.5x the weekday rate.
Consumables (tissue, roll towels, soap, liners) are often billed separately at about $0.012–$0.025 per sq ft per visit if the vendor supplies them.
Equipment such as a compact auto-scrubber may be priced as a monthly rental line if the vendor stages it on-site for the porter.

blocks.text: A porter's output during business hours depends on quiet, compact tools that do not disrupt occupants. A cordless compact auto-scrubber like the Tennant i-mop Lite, with a 14.5-inch cleaning path, 0.8-gallon tank, and 500 RPM twin brushes, lets a porter scrub a restroom core or elevator lobby in minutes without cords across walkways. A quiet dual-rotor mechanical sweeper such as the Rubbermaid Commercial 421288 picks up lobby debris with no noise or power, ideal during meetings. For porters responsible for larger hard-floor corridors above 10,000 sq ft, a 17-inch cordless disk scrubber-dryer like the Clarke Focus II with a 6-gallon tank and AGM batteries covers more ground per pass. Ask vendors whether equipment is included in the hourly rate or itemized.
How to Write a Day Porter Scope That Prices Accurately

items.name: Define coverage hours by traffic peak
items.text: Most offices need porters from 10:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. to cover lunch and the afternoon restroom surge, not a full 8-hour day.

items.name: List recurring rounds with frequencies
items.text: For example: restroom checks every 90 minutes, breakroom reset at 1:30 p.m., lobby glass at 11 a.m.

items.name: Separate on-call duties
items.text: Spill response and conference setups should be listed as priority interrupts so vendors staff correctly.

items.name: Specify consumables and equipment ownership
items.text: State whether you or the vendor supplies paper, soap, liners, and machines.

items.name: Require compliance documentation
items.text: Request a COI, OSHA HazCom training records, and bloodborne pathogens training if porters handle restroom bodily-fluid cleanup.

blocks.title: Watch for idle-hour padding
blocks.text: If a full-time porter quote covers a 15,000 sq ft office with light traffic, the porter will likely spend hours idle or doing nightly-crew work you already pay for. Right-size to part-time and redirect savings to a quarterly deep floor program at $0.03–$0.06 per sq ft per month.

faqs.q: How much does a full-time day porter cost per year?
faqs.a: At $35–$65 per hour for 40 hours per week across 52 weeks (2,080 hours), a full-time day porter costs roughly $72,800–$135,200 per year. That includes the contractor's payroll burden, supervision, and margin. Monthly, at 4.33 weeks per month, it is about $6,062–$11,258.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to hire an in-house porter than contract one?
faqs.a: The wage looks cheaper, but in-house staff carry payroll taxes, workers' compensation, benefits, PTO coverage, OSHA HazCom and bloodborne pathogens training, and replacement when the employee is out. Contractors include backup coverage and insurance with a COI. For most offices under 100,000 sq ft, contracting is cost-competitive once those burdens are counted.

faqs.q: What tasks are excluded from a typical day porter scope?
faqs.a: Common scope exclusions include carpet extraction, VCT strip-and-recoat, exterior window cleaning, biohazard remediation beyond small spills, heavy furniture moves, and post-construction cleanup. Those are billed as project work orders. Confirm exclusions in writing so a porter is not expected to perform specialty work at the standard rate.

faqs.q: Do day porter rates include cleaning supplies and paper products?
faqs.a: Usually the hourly rate includes chemicals and basic tools but not consumables. Paper, soap, and liners are either supplied by the tenant or billed at roughly $0.012–$0.025 per sq ft per visit. Green Seal-certified paper and chemicals may add a modest premium; specify certification requirements in the bid.

faqs.q: Can I start with part-time porter coverage and scale up?
faqs.a: Yes. Most vendors will price a 2- or 4-hour shift with a 30- to 90-day review clause. Track restroom complaints, spill response times, and lobby appearance; if issues cluster outside the covered window, extend hours rather than jumping straight to full-time.
